title: Quality evaluation of scar management information on TikTok: a cross-sectional study
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the 100 most-liked scar management TikTok videos. Alongside the quality instruments (GQS, mDISCERN, PEMAT-A/V, JAMA -- all reported as means, which yield no rows), the paper reports a separate explicit misinformation code with a share of items and a stated denominator: 36% (36/100) of videos contained misinformation. That is a CONTENT row.

estimates.country: Not stated for creators; English-language videos retrieved with an account configured as a 25-year-old user in the United States
estimates.measure_type: % of the 100 most-liked scar management TikTok videos coded as containing misinformation
estimates.denominator: 100 unique English-language TikTok videos on scar management, the top most-liked results across five hashtags (#scartreatment, #scarremoval, #keloid, #hypertrophicscar, #scartherapy), 15 s to 10 min, primary theme scar management
estimates.definition: Video coded as containing misinformation, i.e. medical inaccuracies. The three recorded (non-mutually-exclusive) manifestations were promotion of unproven products (31/100), recommendation of harmful DIY treatment (17/100) and misrepresentation of outcomes (21/100).
estimates.misinfo_def: "Qualitative analysis revealed that these inaccuracies primarily manifested as the promotion of scientifically baseless products, potentially harmful DIY regimens (e.g., abrasive scrubs), and exaggerated treatment outcomes."
estimates.source_quote: Alarmingly, misinformation permeated over one-third (36%) of the entire sample (Table 4).
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 3; the counts are in Table 4 'Misinformation analysis and educational value assessment', p. 5 ("Presence of misinformation, n (%) ... Overall (n = 100): 36 (36.0%)")
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two trained researchers independently evaluated all 100 videos; a consensus meeting resolved scoring discrepancies, with a third senior researcher arbitrating if needed. The only reliability statistic reported is Cohen's kappa = 0.85, and it is stated for the GQS scores, not for the misinformation code. No external fact-check set, clinical guideline benchmark or source-reliability list is named for the misinformation judgement itself; it rests on the two raters' clinical judgement.
estimates.moderator_quote: A purposive sampling strategy was employed to identify the most inﬂuential content within our area of focus. Content was identiﬁed through a systematic query of ﬁve prominent English-language hashtags: scartreatment, scarremoval, keloid, hypertrophicscar, and scartherapy... the search results from each query were sorted by the platform's "most-liked" metric. From these results, the top 100 unique videos that conformed to our eligibility requirements were compiled to form the study's ﬁnal sample.
estimates.notes: denom_selection=curated because the sample is a rank-truncated 'most-liked' top-N, which the authors themselves flag as a survivorship bias ('excluding high-quality educational videos that failed to achieve algorithmic virality') -- so this is a prevalence among highly viral scar content, not among all scar content. country_norm=Global: the videos are English-language from unstated countries; only the retrieval account was configured as a US user, which is a personalisation control, not a creator-country restriction. Note the ABSTRACT reports only the creator subgroup figure ('Misinformation was prevalent in 46.2% of content creator videos'), not the 36% whole-sample figure; I used the whole-sample figure because its denominator is the full sample.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons: (1) Misinformation by CREATOR TYPE (Table 4): healthcare professionals 3/31 (9.7%), content creators 24/52 (46.2%), general users 9/17 (52.9%). These are source-type subgroups of the same measure in the same country x platform cell, not a separate country/platform/measure/definition axis, so under the one-row-per-distinct-estimate rule I kept only the pooled 36%. Flagging because the ABSTRACT headlines the 46.2% creator figure; an adjudicator who wants creator-type splits has the exact counts here. (2) Misinformation SUBTYPES (Table 4, explicitly 'not mutually exclusive'): promotion of unproven products 31 (31.0%), recommendation of harmful DIY treatment 17 (17.0%), misrepresentation of outcomes 21 (21.0%). Overlapping subtypes of the same 36 videos, not stricter definition variants of the whole, and they sum past 36 -- not R8-usable as separate estimates. (3) All four QUALITY instruments are reported as MEANS only, so no QUALITY row is derivable: GQS 3.45 +/- 0.72 (HCP), 2.15 +/- 0.88 (creators), 1.76 +/- 0.68 (general users) on 1-5; mDISCERN 3.51/1.98/1.65 on 0-5; JAMA 3.23/0.44/0.12 on 0-4; PEMAT understandability 88.2%/81.4%/79.5% and actionability 81.5%/55.4%/41.2% (these last are mean percentage scores, i.e. scale scores, not shares of videos). The one threshold-based share, '83.9% [of healthcare professionals' videos] meeting the quality threshold of three', is a creator subgroup only, with no whole-sample equivalent, so no QUALITY row. (4) Table 3 content themes (unproven 'miracle' creams/serums 54%, DIY home remedies 33%, evidence-based treatments 27%) are topic-mention codes, explicitly non-mutually-exclusive, and are not veracity judgements about the video. (5) JAMA authorship/attribution shares are source-transparency, not veracity.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of TikTok. Retrieval standardised with a newly created account (profile set to a 25-year-old US user, no viewing history) to give an algorithm-neutral baseline; data collected 1-7 March 2025 under a pre-defined protocol. Purposive sampling: five English-language hashtags queried, results sorted by 'most-liked', top 100 unique eligible videos retained. Eligibility: English, 15 s-10 min, primary theme scar management; excluded duplicates, non-cutaneous-scar content, and personal stories with no educational advice. Two trained researchers independently coded all 100 videos with a standardised coding sheet; consensus meeting for discrepancies, third senior researcher arbitrating; Cohen's kappa 0.85 reported for GQS. Instruments: mDISCERN, JAMA benchmark, PEMAT-A/V, GQS. Non-parametric analysis (Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman) in SPSS 28. No IRB (public data). Authors' limitations: cross-sectional single time point, English-only, and most-liked sampling introducing survivorship bias; correlational design cannot establish causality and does not control for follower count or video age.
rob.item6_quote: Qualitative analysis revealed that these inaccuracies primarily manifested as the promotion of scientiﬁcally baseless products, potentially harmful DIY regimens (e.g., abrasive scrubs), and exaggerated treatment outcomes.
rob.item10_quote: Alarmingly, misinformation permeated over one-third (36%) of the entire sample (Table 4). While healthcare professionals largely maintained accuracy (9.7% misinformation rate), non-professional creators were signiﬁcant sources of error, with nearly half of their content containing medical inaccuracies (46.2% for creators and 52.9% for general users).
